The check 'correctness-keys-repinned-on-identical-topic-basis' re-derives that comparison from both pinned commits and fails if it ever stops holding.
authored_against: High School Biology, Grade 9. Keys state established science at this course level; they are not extracted from the source, which states a focus and generic objectives.

fixed_facts: Typical bacterial cells are on the order of micrometres; typical eukaryotic cells are tens of micrometres; molecules such as proteins are on the order of nanometres.
relationships: Biological structures span many orders of magnitude, and the appropriate unit and instrument change with the scale being studied.
The scale of a structure constrains what can be observed about it: light microscopy resolves cells and large organelles, not individual proteins.
A measurement is meaningful only with its unit and the method that produced it.
accepted_alternative_framings: Scientific notation, SI prefixes, and explicit unit conversions are all acceptable ways to express biological scale.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming individual protein molecules can be resolved with a light microscope.
Reporting a biological measurement with no unit, or with a unit off by orders of magnitude for the structure named.
Claiming a cell and an organelle are of comparable size.
topics.out_of_scope: Electron microscopy theory, super-resolution methods, and instrument physics are beyond this course.

relationships: Repeated trials estimate how much a measurement varies, which is what makes a difference between conditions interpretable.
Biological variation between individuals is real variation, not measurement error, and the two are reported separately.
A difference smaller than the spread within a condition is not evidence of an effect.
accepted_alternative_framings: Reporting a range, a mean with a spread, or individual trial values are all acceptable at this level.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming an effect from a difference smaller than the variation between replicates.
Treating biological variation between individuals as experimental error to be eliminated.
Reporting a mean with no indication of the spread or the number of trials.
topics.out_of_scope: Formal statistical tests, confidence intervals, and power analysis are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Carbon forms four covalent bonds, which is why it builds the large, varied molecules life depends on.
The four major classes of biological macromolecule are carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids.
relationships: Carbon's capacity to form four stable covalent bonds, including with other carbon atoms, allows chains, branches, and rings, and therefore enormous molecular variety.
Carbohydrates, proteins, and nucleic acids are polymers built from repeating monomers; lipids are not polymers in the same sense.
Monomers are joined by removing water and separated by adding it.
accepted_alternative_framings: Naming the joining and splitting reactions dehydration synthesis and hydrolysis, or describing them as removing and adding water, are equally correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming carbon forms a number of covalent bonds other than four in these molecules.
Claiming lipids are polymers of a repeating monomer in the way proteins and nucleic acids are.
Claiming monomers are joined by adding water and separated by removing it.
topics.out_of_scope: Detailed organic reaction mechanisms and stereochemistry are Chemistry course work.

relationships: The three-dimensional shape and chemical properties of a biological molecule determine what it can interact with and therefore what it does.
Changing the structure changes the function, which is why a small change in shape can abolish activity entirely.
The relationship runs from structure to function; a molecule does not acquire a structure because a function is needed.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a molecule changes its structure in order to perform a function it is required to perform.
Claiming function can be predicted from composition without regard to structure.
Claiming structure and function are independent.
topics.out_of_scope: Structural biology methods and molecular dynamics are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: An enzyme lowers the activation energy of a reaction and is not consumed by it.
Enzymes do not change whether a reaction is energetically favourable; they change how fast it proceeds.
relationships: An enzyme is a biological catalyst: it lowers activation energy, speeds the reaction, and emerges unchanged.
Enzyme activity depends on temperature and pH, rising to an optimum and falling away as the enzyme's shape is disrupted.
Specificity comes from the shape and chemistry of the active site, which is why an enzyme acts on particular substrates.
accepted_alternative_framings: Lock-and-key and induced-fit descriptions are both acceptable; induced fit is the more accurate model.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming an enzyme is used up in the reaction it catalyses.
Claiming an enzyme makes an energetically unfavourable reaction favourable.
Claiming high temperature always increases enzyme activity, ignoring denaturation.
topics.out_of_scope: Enzyme kinetics, Michaelis-Menten parameters, and inhibition types are beyond this course.

relationships: A biological argument links a claim to evidence through explicit reasoning about mechanism or pattern.
Biological systems are variable, so an argument states how much of the observed pattern the evidence actually establishes.
The strongest alternative explanation is stated and addressed rather than omitted.
disqualifying_errors: Inferring a causal mechanism from a correlation with no further evidence.
Generalising from a single organism or a single trial to a population.
Omitting evidence or an alternative explanation that weakens the claim.
topics.out_of_scope: Formal experimental design theory and meta-analysis are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine.
DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel strands with a sugar-phosphate backbone on the outside and paired bases on the inside.
relationships: DNA is composed of nucleotides, each a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group, and one of four nitrogenous bases.
The two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases: adenine with thymine, guanine with cytosine.
Because the pairing is complementary, each strand specifies the sequence of the other, which is what makes accurate copying possible.
accepted_alternative_framings: Writing the pairing as A-T and G-C, or spelling out the base names, are equally correct.
disqualifying_errors: Pairing adenine with guanine, or cytosine with thymine.
Claiming the bases form the backbone and the sugars and phosphates lie in the interior.
Claiming the two strands run in the same direction.
topics.out_of_scope: Base-stacking energetics, DNA topology, and chromatin structure in detail are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: DNA replication is semiconservative: each new double helix contains one original strand and one newly made strand.
relationships: The double helix separates and each original strand acts as a template for a new complementary strand.
Because replication is semiconservative, every daughter molecule retains one parental strand.
Copying is highly accurate but not perfect, and uncorrected errors become mutations.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing the template as the parental strand, or as the original strand, are equally correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming replication is conservative, with the original helix intact and a wholly new one produced.
Claiming the new strand has the same sequence as its template rather than the complementary sequence.
Claiming replication is error-free.
topics.out_of_scope: Replication fork enzymology, leading and lagging strand detail, and telomere biology are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Transcription copies a DNA sequence into RNA; RNA contains uracil in place of thymine and ribose in place of deoxyribose.
In eukaryotes transcription occurs in the nucleus and translation occurs at ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
relationships: Transcription produces a single-stranded RNA copy complementary to one DNA strand.
Only part of the genome is transcribed in any given cell at any given time, which is why cells with identical DNA differ.
The messenger RNA carries the sequence information out of the nucleus to the ribosome.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing the copied strand as the template or non-coding strand is correct; naming the other strand the coding or sense strand is also correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming RNA contains thymine.
Claiming transcription produces protein.
Claiming every gene is transcribed in every cell at all times.
topics.out_of_scope: Promoter structure, splicing detail, and transcription factor biochemistry are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: The genetic code is read in three-nucleotide codons, and it is redundant: most amino acids are specified by more than one codon.
Proteins are built from twenty standard amino acids.
relationships: Ribosomes read messenger RNA in codons of three nucleotides and assemble the corresponding amino acids into a chain.
Transfer RNA molecules match codons to amino acids, which is how the nucleotide sequence is converted into an amino acid sequence.
The code is redundant but not ambiguous: one codon specifies one amino acid, while one amino acid may have several codons.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing the code as degenerate or as redundant are the same claim.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming one nucleotide, or two, specifies one amino acid.
Claiming each amino acid has exactly one codon.
Claiming translation occurs in the nucleus in eukaryotic cells.
topics.out_of_scope: Ribosome structure, elongation factor biochemistry, and codon usage bias are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: A protein's amino acid sequence, together with its cellular environment, determines the three-dimensional structure it folds into, and that structure determines its function.
relationships: The order of amino acids determines how the chain folds, because the side chains interact with each other and with water.
A protein that loses its folded shape loses its function, which is what denaturation by heat or extreme pH does.
Because structure follows from sequence, a change in the sequence can change or abolish the function.
accepted_alternative_framings: Referring to primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary structure is correct but not required.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a protein's function is determined by its amino acid composition regardless of order.
Claiming a denatured protein retains its function because its sequence is unchanged.
Claiming proteins fold into shapes that are chosen to suit the function required.
topics.out_of_scope: Chaperone biology, folding thermodynamics, and structure prediction are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: A mutation is a change in DNA sequence; its effect may be harmful, beneficial, or neutral, and depends on where it occurs and what it changes.
relationships: Mutations arise from replication errors and from chemical and radiation damage, and most are repaired.
A substitution may change no amino acid, change one, or introduce a stop; an insertion or deletion that is not a multiple of three shifts the reading frame and usually has a larger effect.
Only mutations in the germ line are inherited; somatic mutations affect the individual alone.
accepted_alternative_framings: Silent, missense, nonsense, and frameshift are correct names; describing the effect without the labels is equally acceptable.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming all mutations are harmful.
Claiming mutations occur because the organism or population needs a particular change.
Claiming a somatic mutation is passed to offspring.
topics.out_of_scope: Repair pathway biochemistry and mutational signature analysis are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: All living organisms are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and all cells come from pre-existing cells.
Prokaryotic cells have no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells have both.
relationships: Cell theory holds that organisms are composed of cells, that the cell is the basic unit of structure and function, and that cells arise only from existing cells.
Prokaryotic cells lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and a range of organelles.
Both cell types have a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, and DNA.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming prokaryotic cells have no DNA or no ribosomes.
Claiming viruses are cells or are alive by the criteria of cell theory.
Claiming cells can arise spontaneously from non-living material under present conditions.
topics.out_of_scope: Endosymbiotic theory in detail and archaeal biology are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: The nucleus holds the genetic material, ribosomes assemble proteins, mitochondria carry out most ATP production, and chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis in plant cells.
relationships: Organelles are specialised compartments whose functions depend on one another, so the cell operates as an integrated system.
Membranes create separate chemical environments, which is what allows incompatible processes to run in the same cell at once.
A product of one organelle is frequently the input of another, so disrupting one disrupts others.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming plant cells have chloroplasts instead of mitochondria; plant cells have both.
Claiming mitochondria produce energy rather than converting it into a usable chemical form.
Claiming organelles function independently of one another.
topics.out_of_scope: Vesicular trafficking detail and organelle proteomics are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: The hierarchy runs cells, tissues, organs, organ systems, organism.
relationships: Specialised cells of similar type form tissues; tissues combine into organs; organs work together as organ systems.
Each level shows capabilities the level below does not have on its own, which is what makes the hierarchy meaningful.
Organ systems are interdependent, so a failure in one propagates to others.
disqualifying_errors: Placing the levels of organisation out of order.
Claiming an organ consists of a single tissue type.
Claiming organ systems operate independently.
topics.out_of_scope: Histology and comparative anatomy are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Mitosis produces two daughter cells genetically identical to the parent cell and to each other.
DNA is replicated during interphase, before mitosis begins.
relationships: The cell cycle consists of interphase, during which the cell grows and replicates its DNA, followed by division.
Mitosis distributes one complete copy of the replicated chromosomes to each daughter cell, so chromosome number is maintained.
Checkpoints regulate progression, and loss of that regulation underlies uncontrolled division.
accepted_alternative_framings: Naming the mitotic stages is correct but not required; describing the outcome accurately is what matters here.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming mitosis halves the chromosome number.
Claiming DNA is replicated during mitosis itself rather than during interphase.
Claiming mitosis produces genetically varied daughter cells.
topics.out_of_scope: Cyclin and checkpoint kinase biochemistry, and cancer genetics, are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Differentiated cells in one organism generally contain the same genome; they differ in which genes are expressed.
relationships: Differentiation is the process by which cells become specialised, and it results from differences in gene expression rather than differences in the genes present.
Stem cells retain the capacity to divide and to give rise to specialised cell types.
Because the genome is retained, differentiation is about regulation, not about loss of genetic information.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming differentiated cells have lost the genes they do not use.
Claiming every cell in the body expresses the same genes.
Claiming differentiation is driven by the cell choosing what the organism needs.
topics.out_of_scope: Reprogramming methods, epigenetic mechanisms in detail, and stem-cell therapeutics are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: As an object grows with its shape unchanged, its volume increases faster than its surface area, so the surface-area-to-volume ratio falls.
relationships: Exchange with the environment happens across the surface, while demand scales with volume, so cells are limited in the size they can reach.
Multicellular organisms overcome the limit with many small cells and with structures such as folds, villi, and branching that increase surface area.
The ratio explains why cells divide rather than simply growing larger.
accepted_alternative_framings: Explaining the constraint through diffusion distance, or through the ratio of surface to volume, are both correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming surface area and volume increase in the same proportion as an object grows.
Claiming a larger cell exchanges materials more efficiently than a smaller one.
Claiming the ratio increases as a cell grows.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative diffusion modelling and allometric scaling laws are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Homeostasis maintains internal conditions within a tolerance range, not at a single unchanging value.
relationships: A regulated variable has a setpoint and a range within which the organism functions.
Values fluctuate within the range continuously; regulation acts when a departure is detected, so variation is expected.
Different variables have different ranges, and exceeding a range has consequences specific to that variable.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a homeostatically regulated variable is held perfectly constant.
Treating any fluctuation within the tolerance range as a regulatory failure.
Claiming all regulated variables share one tolerance range.
topics.out_of_scope: Control theory and quantitative physiological modelling are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Negative feedback opposes the change that triggered it and returns the variable toward its setpoint.
relationships: A negative feedback loop requires a sensor that detects the change, a control centre that compares it with the setpoint, and an effector that acts to reverse it.
Because the response opposes the deviation, the system is stabilised around the setpoint.
Most physiological regulation, including of body temperature, blood glucose, and water balance, is negative feedback.
accepted_alternative_framings: Naming the three components sensor, control centre, and effector, or receptor, integrator, and effector, are equally correct.
disqualifying_errors: Describing a loop as negative feedback when the response amplifies the original change.
Omitting the detection step and claiming the effector acts on its own.
Claiming negative feedback means the outcome is harmful.
topics.out_of_scope: Gain, time constants, and formal control-system analysis are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Positive feedback amplifies the change that triggered it and drives the system away from the starting condition.
relationships: In positive feedback the response reinforces the original change rather than opposing it.
Positive feedback drives processes to completion, such as childbirth, blood clotting, and the rising phase of a nerve impulse.
Positive feedback requires an external stopping condition, because the loop itself does not stabilise.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming positive feedback means a beneficial outcome and negative feedback a harmful one.
Describing a stabilising loop as positive feedback.
Claiming positive feedback maintains a setpoint.
topics.out_of_scope: Bistability and formal dynamical systems analysis are beyond this course.

relationships: Disease can result when a sensor, a control centre, an effector, or the signal between them fails.
The same symptom can arise from failures at different points in the loop, so the symptom alone does not identify the cause.
Treatment that replaces an effector's output does not restore regulation unless the loop can still detect and respond.
disqualifying_errors: Inferring the point of failure from the symptom alone with no further evidence.
Claiming a failure at any point in the loop produces the same physiological effect.
Claiming replacing a hormone restores feedback regulation as well as the hormone level.
topics.out_of_scope: Clinical diagnosis, pharmacology, and specific disease mechanisms in depth are beyond this course.

relationships: Regulating one variable usually involves several organ systems acting together, coordinated by nervous and endocrine signals.
Nervous signalling is fast and short-lived; endocrine signalling is slower and more sustained, and the two are used for different regulatory jobs.
Because systems are coupled, correcting one variable can disturb another.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a single organ regulates a variable without involving others.
Claiming nervous and endocrine signalling operate on the same timescale.
Claiming correcting one regulated variable never affects any other.
topics.out_of_scope: Specific hormone axes in detail and integrative physiology modelling are beyond this course.

relationships: A quantitative feedback model represents the variable over time, the setpoint, and the size and delay of the response.
Delay in the response produces oscillation around the setpoint rather than a smooth return.
A model is evaluated against measured time-course data, not against how reasonable it looks.
accepted_alternative_framings: Graphical, tabular, and equation-based representations are all acceptable model forms here.
disqualifying_errors: Modelling a regulated variable as returning instantly to setpoint with no delay or overshoot.
Presenting a model output as though it were measured data.
Claiming a model is validated without comparison to data.
topics.out_of_scope: Differential equation modelling and parameter estimation are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Chlorophyll absorbs light most strongly in the blue and red regions and reflects green, which is why plants appear green.
relationships: Pigments absorb particular wavelengths of light and transfer that energy into the photosynthetic process.
Light absorbed is used; light reflected or transmitted is not, which is why leaf colour indicates which wavelengths are least used.
The light-dependent reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast.
accepted_alternative_framings: Naming accessory pigments such as carotenoids alongside chlorophyll is correct and not required.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming chlorophyll absorbs green light most strongly.
Claiming plants take in light and store it as light energy.
Claiming photosynthesis occurs in the mitochondria.
topics.out_of_scope: Photosystem biochemistry, electron transport detail, and absorption spectra analysis are beyond this course.

topics.focus: photosynthesis as matter and energy transformation
fixed_facts: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water, with light energy, to produce glucose and oxygen.
The oxygen released by photosynthesis comes from water, not from carbon dioxide.
relationships: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in the bonds of sugar.
The carbon in the sugar comes from atmospheric carbon dioxide, which is the origin of most of a plant's mass.
Photosynthesis is both an energy transformation and a matter transformation, and a complete account addresses both.
accepted_alternative_framings: Writing the overall equation in words or in symbols, and naming the light-dependent reactions and the Calvin cycle, are all acceptable.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming the oxygen released comes from carbon dioxide.
Claiming a plant's mass comes principally from the soil.
Claiming photosynthesis creates energy rather than converting it.
topics.out_of_scope: Calvin cycle intermediates, RuBisCO kinetics, and photorespiration are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Aerobic cellular respiration uses glucose and oxygen and produces carbon dioxide, water, and ATP.
Cellular respiration occurs in all living cells, including plant cells.
relationships: Cellular respiration releases energy stored in glucose and captures it in ATP, the cell's usable energy currency.
Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm; the remaining aerobic stages occur in the mitochondria.
Respiration is not the reverse of photosynthesis in mechanism, although the overall inputs and outputs are complementary.
accepted_alternative_framings: Naming the stages glycolysis, the Krebs or citric acid cycle, and the electron transport chain is correct but not required.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming plants carry out photosynthesis instead of respiration.
Claiming respiration produces energy rather than transferring stored chemical energy into ATP.
Claiming cellular respiration and breathing are the same process.
topics.out_of_scope: ATP yield accounting in detail, chemiosmosis, and proton gradient biophysics are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Anaerobic pathways yield far less ATP per glucose molecule than aerobic respiration.
relationships: When oxygen is unavailable, cells use anaerobic pathways such as lactic acid fermentation or alcoholic fermentation.
Fermentation regenerates the molecules glycolysis needs to continue, which is why it allows ATP production to keep going.
The far lower ATP yield is why anaerobic activity cannot be sustained for long at high demand.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing fermentation's role as regenerating NAD+, or as allowing glycolysis to continue, are both correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming fermentation produces more ATP than aerobic respiration.
Claiming fermentation produces no ATP at all.
Claiming lactic acid accumulation is what causes delayed-onset muscle soreness.
topics.out_of_scope: Detailed fermentation biochemistry and exercise physiology are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Atoms are conserved through every metabolic process; they are rearranged, never created or destroyed.
relationships: The atoms in an organism's body came from the food, water, and gases it took in.
Tracing an element through metabolism means following where its atoms go, and every atom is accounted for.
Mass lost by an organism leaves as matter, principally as exhaled carbon dioxide and as water, not as energy.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming atoms are consumed or destroyed during metabolism.
Claiming body mass lost is converted into energy and thereby ceases to be matter.
Claiming an organism builds tissue from matter that did not enter it.
topics.out_of_scope: Isotope tracer methodology and metabolic flux analysis are beyond this course.

relationships: Energy taken in is used for maintenance, growth, movement, and reproduction, with a substantial fraction released to the surroundings as thermal energy.
Energy is conserved: an account balances intake against use, storage, and loss.
Because energy is degraded to thermal energy at every transfer, organisms need a continuous supply.
disqualifying_errors: Presenting an energy account in which energy is created or destroyed.
Claiming all energy taken in is available for growth.
Claiming energy, like matter, is recycled within the organism.
topics.out_of_scope: Calorimetry, metabolic rate measurement, and quantitative energy budgets are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Only a small fraction of the energy at one trophic level, on the order of ten per cent, is incorporated into the next.
relationships: Energy enters most ecosystems through producers and passes upward through consumers, with most released as thermal energy at each transfer.
Because so little energy passes upward, food chains have few levels and higher levels support far less biomass.
Energy flows through an ecosystem in one direction and is not recycled.
accepted_alternative_framings: Approximate statements such as 'about ten per cent' or 'roughly a tenth' are correct; an exact figure is not.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming energy cycles through an ecosystem the way matter does.
Claiming most of the energy at one trophic level passes to the next.
Claiming a long food chain supports as much biomass at the top as at the bottom.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative production ecology and ecological efficiency measurement are beyond this course.

relationships: Food web arrows point from the organism consumed to the consumer, showing the direction matter and energy move.
Matter cycles within the ecosystem; the atoms in a consumer were previously in its food and will later be elsewhere.
Because organisms occupy multiple positions in a web, effects of a change propagate beyond the direct link.
disqualifying_errors: Drawing food-web arrows from consumer to consumed.
Claiming matter is used up and lost from the ecosystem.
Claiming removing a species affects only the species directly linked to it.
topics.out_of_scope: Network analysis metrics and quantitative food-web modelling are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Photosynthesis moves carbon from the atmosphere into organisms; respiration, decomposition, and combustion return it.
relationships: Carbon moves between the atmosphere, organisms, soil, water, and rock, and the timescales of those movements differ by orders of magnitude.
Fossil fuel combustion transfers carbon from a long-term geological reservoir into the atmosphere far faster than natural processes return it.
A carbon cycle account balances the flows in and out of each reservoir.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming carbon is created or destroyed as it moves through the cycle.
Claiming only plants and animals participate in the carbon cycle.
Claiming the fast biological cycle and the slow geological cycle operate at comparable rates.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative reservoir sizes, flux measurements, and ocean carbonate chemistry are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Atmospheric nitrogen gas cannot be used directly by plants or animals; it must first be fixed into usable compounds.
relationships: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria, and industrial processes, convert atmospheric nitrogen into forms plants can take up.
Nitrogen moves from soil to plants to consumers and back through excretion and decomposition.
Adding excess nutrients to water bodies stimulates growth that, on decomposing, depletes dissolved oxygen.
accepted_alternative_framings: Naming the steps fixation, nitrification, assimilation, ammonification, and denitrification is correct but not required.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming plants take nitrogen directly from the air.
Claiming animals obtain nitrogen from the atmosphere.
Claiming adding more nutrients to an ecosystem always improves it.
topics.out_of_scope: Detailed microbial biochemistry and nutrient-loading models are beyond this course.

relationships: Decomposers break down dead organisms and waste, returning elements to soil, water, and air in forms producers can use.
Decomposition rate depends on temperature, moisture, oxygen availability, and the material itself.
Without decomposition, matter would remain locked in dead material and nutrient cycling would halt.
accepted_alternative_framings: Naming bacteria, fungi, and detritivores as the agents are all correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming dead material disappears without any organism acting on it.
Claiming decomposers are outside the ecosystem's energy and matter flows.
Claiming decomposition proceeds at the same rate in all conditions.
topics.out_of_scope: Soil biogeochemistry and litter decomposition modelling are beyond this course.

relationships: A quantitative ecosystem model represents stocks and flows of matter or energy and must balance.
Model outputs are conditional on the assumptions and parameter values used, and those are stated.
A model is evaluated against measured data, and disagreement is information about the assumptions.
disqualifying_errors: Presenting model output as though it were measured data.
Reporting a model result without stating its assumptions.
Building a matter or energy model whose inputs and outputs do not balance.
topics.out_of_scope: Sensitivity analysis and formal model validation methods are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Exponential growth has no limiting factor and cannot be sustained; logistic growth slows as the population approaches carrying capacity.
relationships: A population grows exponentially when resources are effectively unlimited, with growth rate proportional to population size.
As resources become limiting, per-individual growth rate declines and the curve levels off near the carrying capacity.
No real population grows exponentially indefinitely, because no environment supplies unlimited resources.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing the curves as J-shaped and S-shaped is correct and equivalent.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a population can sustain exponential growth indefinitely.
Claiming logistic growth means the population stops changing once it reaches carrying capacity.
Confusing the growth rate with the population size.
topics.out_of_scope: Differential equation forms, intrinsic rate of increase, and age-structured models are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Carrying capacity is the population size an environment can sustain given its limiting resources, and it changes when those resources change.
relationships: The limiting factor is the resource in shortest supply relative to demand; increasing any other resource does not raise the population.
Density-dependent factors such as competition, disease, and predation intensify as population rises; density-independent factors such as weather do not.
Carrying capacity is a property of the environment and the population together, and it is not fixed.
disqualifying_errors: Treating carrying capacity as a permanent fixed number for a place.
Claiming increasing a non-limiting resource raises the sustainable population.
Classifying weather events as density-dependent factors.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative estimation of carrying capacity and metapopulation theory are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: In mutualism both species benefit; in commensalism one benefits and the other is essentially unaffected; in parasitism and predation one benefits at the other's expense; in competition both are harmed.
relationships: Interactions are classified by the effect on each participant, not by intent or by how the relationship appears.
Interspecific competition occurs where species use the same limiting resource, and it can shift the resources each species uses.
Predator and prey populations influence one another, typically with a delay between the change in one and the response of the other.
disqualifying_errors: Classifying a relationship as mutualism when only one participant benefits.
Claiming predators normally drive their prey to extinction.
Claiming competition occurs only between members of different species.
topics.out_of_scope: Competitive exclusion modelling and niche partitioning theory in depth are beyond this course.

relationships: Biodiversity measures include the number of species present and how evenly individuals are distributed among them.
A measurement depends on the area sampled, the effort spent, and the method used, so figures are comparable only when those match.
Genetic diversity within species and diversity of ecosystems are also components of biodiversity.
accepted_alternative_framings: Species richness and species evenness are distinct measures, and either or both may be reported.
disqualifying_errors: Comparing biodiversity figures from different sampling areas or methods as though they were equivalent.
Treating species richness as the whole of biodiversity.
Claiming an unsampled species is absent.
topics.out_of_scope: Diversity indices, rarefaction curves, and estimator statistics are beyond this course.

relationships: Disturbance is a normal component of ecosystem dynamics, and many communities depend on it.
Resilience is the capacity to recover ecosystem function after disturbance, and it generally rises with biodiversity.
Severe or repeated disturbance can shift an ecosystem into a different state that does not return on its own.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming all disturbance damages ecosystems.
Claiming an ecosystem always returns to its prior state after disturbance.
Claiming resilience means the ecosystem is unchanged by disturbance.
topics.out_of_scope: Alternative stable state theory and quantitative resilience metrics are beyond this course.

relationships: Group behaviours such as flocking, herding, cooperative hunting, and colonial nesting can increase individual survival and reproductive success.
Group living also imposes costs, including competition within the group and faster transmission of disease and parasites.
Whether group behaviour is favoured depends on the balance of those costs and benefits in the specific environment.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming group behaviour evolves for the good of the species irrespective of effects on individuals.
Claiming group living carries benefits with no costs.
Claiming animals adopt group behaviour because they understand its advantages.
topics.out_of_scope: Kin selection, inclusive fitness calculations, and game-theoretic models are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: A gene occupies a specific locus on a specific chromosome, and different versions of a gene at that locus are alleles.
relationships: Genes occupy fixed positions on chromosomes, and homologous chromosomes carry the same genes at the same loci.
Diploid organisms carry two copies of each locus, one from each parent, and those copies may be the same allele or different alleles.
Genes close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together.
disqualifying_errors: Using gene and allele as interchangeable terms.
Claiming homologous chromosomes carry identical DNA sequences.
Claiming every gene is on a different chromosome from every other.
topics.out_of_scope: Linkage mapping, recombination frequencies, and chromosome banding are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Meiosis halves the chromosome number and produces four genetically distinct haploid cells from one diploid cell.
relationships: Meiosis involves two divisions after a single round of DNA replication, which is why the chromosome number is halved.
Crossing over between homologous chromosomes, and the independent assortment of homologous pairs, produce genetically distinct gametes.
Fertilisation restores the diploid number and adds a further source of combination.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming meiosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells.
Claiming meiosis maintains the chromosome number rather than halving it.
Claiming DNA is replicated between the first and second meiotic divisions.
topics.out_of_scope: Synaptonemal complex biology and nondisjunction mechanisms in detail are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: The sources of heritable variation are mutation, recombination during meiosis, independent assortment, and the random combination of gametes at fertilisation.
relationships: Mutation is the ultimate source of new alleles; the other mechanisms rearrange existing alleles into new combinations.
Sexual reproduction generates far more genetic variety among offspring than asexual reproduction does.
Variation is present in a population before selection acts on it.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming recombination creates new alleles.
Claiming variation arises in response to environmental need.
Claiming asexual reproduction produces the same level of genetic variety as sexual reproduction.
topics.out_of_scope: Population genetics and allele frequency mathematics are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: A Punnett square gives expected proportions across many offspring, not an outcome for any individual offspring.
relationships: A Punnett square enumerates the possible gamete combinations and their expected frequencies.
Each fertilisation is an independent event, so previous offspring do not change the probabilities for the next.
Observed proportions in small samples deviate from expectation by chance, and that deviation is not evidence against the model.
accepted_alternative_framings: Punnett squares, probability rules, and branch diagrams give the same predictions and are all acceptable.
disqualifying_errors: Reading a three-to-one expected ratio as a guarantee about four offspring.
Claiming previous offspring change the probability for a subsequent one.
Rejecting a genetic model because a small family departed from the expected ratio.
topics.out_of_scope: Chi-squared goodness-of-fit testing is beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Many traits are influenced by multiple genes and by the environment, and these show continuous rather than discrete variation.
relationships: A polygenic trait is influenced by several genes, each contributing part of the effect, which produces a continuous range of phenotypes.
The environment modifies the expression of many traits, so genotype does not determine phenotype on its own.
Simple dominant-recessive models apply to a minority of traits and mislead when applied to polygenic ones.
disqualifying_errors: Modelling a continuously varying trait such as height as a single gene with two alleles and presenting the result as established.
Claiming genotype fully determines phenotype regardless of environment.
Claiming an environmentally induced change in an individual is inherited through the genome.
topics.out_of_scope: Heritability estimation, quantitative trait loci, and genome-wide association methods are beyond this course.

relationships: Traits influenced by many genes and by the environment are distributed continuously in a population, often clustering around a central value.
The distribution is a property of the population, and no individual measurement characterises it.
Comparing distributions requires comparable measurement methods and sample sizes.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing the shape as a normal or bell-shaped distribution is correct; describing it in plain terms is equally acceptable.
disqualifying_errors: Drawing a conclusion about a population's trait distribution from one individual.
Claiming a continuous trait falls into discrete categories because the data was binned that way.
Comparing trait distributions measured by different methods as though they were equivalent.
topics.out_of_scope: Descriptive and inferential statistics beyond reading a distribution are beyond this course.

topics.focus: multiple lines of evidence for common ancestry
fixed_facts: Evidence for common ancestry comes from the fossil record, comparative anatomy, embryology, biogeography, and molecular sequence comparison.
relationships: Independent lines of evidence converging on the same pattern of relationship is what makes common ancestry a robust conclusion.
Shared DNA and protein sequences among species match the pattern inferred from anatomy and fossils.
Shared underlying structure used for different functions indicates common ancestry; similar function achieved by different structures does not.
accepted_alternative_framings: Naming homologous and analogous structures is correct but not required, provided the distinction is used correctly.
disqualifying_errors: Treating similarity of function as evidence of close relationship.
Claiming a single line of evidence establishes the relationships on its own.
Claiming one living species is the ancestor of another living species.
topics.out_of_scope: Phylogenetic tree-building algorithms and molecular clock calibration are beyond this course.

topics.focus: the four factors driving natural selection
fixed_facts: Natural selection requires: more offspring produced than can survive; heritable variation among individuals; competition for limited resources; and differential survival and reproduction of individuals with particular heritable traits.
relationships: All four conditions are necessary; if any is absent, natural selection does not operate.
Selection acts on phenotypes, and the effect is heritable only to the extent that the variation is genetic.
The outcome is a change in the frequency of heritable traits in the population across generations.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing the fourth factor as differential reproductive success, or as differences in survival and reproduction, are equivalent.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming individual organisms evolve or adapt themselves during their lifetimes.
Claiming variation arises because the population needs it.
Claiming natural selection has a goal, a direction toward complexity, or an endpoint.
topics.out_of_scope: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, genetic drift quantification, and speciation modelling are beyond this course.

relationships: Selection is detected as a change in the distribution of a trait in a population over generations.
A shift in a distribution is evidence about the population, not about any individual within it.
The strength of the evidence depends on sample size, on measurement method, and on the number of generations observed.
accepted_alternative_framings: Directional, stabilising, and disruptive selection are correct names for the distributional patterns; describing the shift without the labels is equally acceptable.
disqualifying_errors: Inferring selection from a change in one individual.
Claiming a shift in a trait distribution is necessarily due to selection, without considering other causes.
Reporting a distributional change with no reference to sample size or generations.
topics.out_of_scope: Selection coefficients and formal statistical inference are beyond this course.

fixed_facts: Adaptation is a population-level outcome across generations, not a change an individual makes during its life.
relationships: An adaptation is a heritable trait that has become common in a population because it improved survival and reproduction in that environment.
A trait that is adaptive in one environment can be neutral or harmful in another, so adaptation is always relative to conditions.
Not every trait is an adaptation; some persist through chance, through linkage to other traits, or as by-products.
disqualifying_errors: Describing an individual organism as adapting to its environment during its lifetime as an evolutionary process.
Claiming every trait an organism has is an adaptation.
Claiming an adaptation is a trait the organism developed because it was needed.
topics.out_of_scope: Adaptationist critique, exaptation theory, and comparative methods are beyond this course.

relationships: When the environment changes, populations may shift in trait frequency, migrate, or become extinct, and which occurs depends on existing variation and the rate of change.
Rapid change is more likely to cause extinction than gradual change, because there is less opportunity for trait frequencies to shift.
Extinction is the normal fate of most species over geological time, and the fossil record documents this.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a population will always evolve in time to survive an environmental change.
Claiming extinction indicates a defect in the organisms rather than a mismatch with changed conditions.
Claiming populations can evolve traits for which no variation exists.
topics.out_of_scope: Extinction rate estimation and mass extinction mechanisms in detail are beyond this course.

relationships: Interventions to protect biodiversity are evaluated against stated criteria and against evidence of effect, not against intent.
Because ecosystems are connected, an intervention has effects beyond its target, sometimes delayed or distant.
Monitoring after the intervention is what converts an expected effect into an observed one.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming an intervention affects only its intended target.
Declaring an intervention successful without post-intervention monitoring.
Presenting a conservation option as having benefits with no costs or trade-offs.
topics.out_of_scope: Conservation policy, environmental impact assessment procedure, and economic valuation are beyond this course.
